paragraphs.source_en: His wife said, “We shall be short this month...” “There is no reason we should be short. I have paid the doctor for the medicine, and did I not settle the account with the bookseller last month? There ought to be money left over this month.” The master replied with complete unconcern. At the same time he gazed upon the nose hairs he had plucked out as though they were a wonder of the world. “But you do not eat rice; you eat bread and jam.” “How many tins of jam have I eaten, then?” “Eight tins altogether this month.” “Eight tins? I have no recollection of eating anything like that many.” “It is not only you who eat it. The children eat it too.” “Even if we did eat that much, it would come to only five or six yen.” As he said this, the master, quite unperturbed, carefully planted the nose hairs one by one on the manuscript paper; because a bit of flesh clung to their roots, they stood upright on the page like needles. The master seemed deeply moved by this unexpected discovery and gave them a puff. They stuck so firmly that they would not budge at all. “Confoundedly stubborn,” said the master. And he blew with all his might again. His wife, her cheeks swelling with indignation, said, “It is not only jam. There are other things we simply have to buy.” “Perhaps there are,” the master said indifferently. As he spoke, he thrust his fingers back into his nostril and yanked out another nose hair. Among those black, red, and variously colored nose hairs, there was one that was completely white. The master seemed greatly startled; he stared at it without blinking, then held the hair between two fingers and brought it up before his wife’s face. His wife frowned, pushed his hand back, and said, “How disgusting!” “Just look at it. Even my nose hairs are turning white!” The master appeared to be overcome with feeling. His wife, who had originally come to discuss serious business, could only withdraw to the sitting room with a laugh. It seemed she had given up trying to consult the master about household finances. The master returned once more to his Natural Layman.

paragraphs.source_en: Having driven his wife away with nose hairs, the master seemed to feel he could now be at ease; he was impatient to pluck out one more nose hair and then write a sentence, but the more urgently he tried to set brush to paper, the less the brush would move. He muttered to himself, “‘Eats roasted sweet potatoes’ seems superfluous too. I shall make the painful sacrifice.” So saying, he crossed out those words as well. “‘One stick of incense’ is too abrupt as well. Away with it!” Without the least regret, the master executed those words too with his brush. All that remained was: “Natural Layman is a man who studies space and reads The Analects.” The master again felt this was perhaps too simple. “Oh, what a bother! I shall not write an essay; I shall write only an epitaph.” He swept his great brush left and right, making two strokes across the manuscript paper like the orchids in a clumsy literati painting, and the composition he had labored over so strenuously was condemned without a single character surviving. Then he turned the paper over and wrote a passage of obscure meaning: “Born in space, he investigated space, and died in space. O space, O interval, Natural Layman, ah!” At that moment Meitei drifted in, as usual. Meitei was the sort of man who perhaps regarded other people’s houses as his own; without so much as announcing himself, he would stride in quite unceremoniously. Nor was that all: at times he would even drift in through the kitchen door at the back of the house. He was a man who, from birth, had dropped somewhere far away all such things as worry, reserve, embarrassment, and trouble-taking.
